title: 10 Settings, the child lock and putting things back

steps.say: This lesson shows how Settings keeps choices, how the child lock works, and how any change can be put back.

steps.anchor: /* Settings: a sidebar of pages, drawn in the design's own type and colours.
steps.through: * how the desktop looks, into the design itself), and comes back at boot. */
steps.say: Settings is drawn in the person's own design. Each choice takes effect at once and is kept for the next start.
The pages are a plain list: a title, an icon and the function that draws the page. Pages that other parts add with `settings_register_page` go between AI and Users.
Every setting goes through `settings_set`, into /etc/os/settings.conf. Note the limit: it holds 48 keys, and a new key past that is quietly dropped.

steps.anchor: changes_note_setting(key, kv[i].val, value); /* (kept, to be put back: changes.c) */
steps.say: Before a value changes, the old one is written down. That is what makes putting it back possible.

steps.anchor: /* What changed, kept so it can be put back (changes.c): every setting chosen (settings_set) and every change to
steps.through: * locked, not even on a child's computer. */
steps.say: The last thirty changes are kept, settings and designs both. The companion is told the recent ones. If someone seems upset after a change, it offers to put it back, and does so only on their yes.

steps.anchor: while ((o = strstr(m->text, "[[putback"))) { /* a change put back, on their yes (changes.c): never locked */
steps.say: It does that with a `[[putback]]` tag in its reply, which `changes_put_back` carries out. A design is restored from the copy kept in /etc/os/changes.

steps.anchor: /* The child lock (family.c): a computer a grown-up set up for a child. What is locked and the grown-up's password
steps.through: * When something locked is asked for, a small box asks for the grown-up's password; once typed, the computer
steps.say: The **child lock** is for a computer a grown-up set up for a child. Five things can be locked: time, the web, Settings and the design, installing apps, and what the companion may do.

steps.anchor: void family_ask(const char *doing, void (*then)(const char *arg), const char *arg);
steps.say: Code that does something locked calls `family_ask`. It shows the password box and carries on only once the grown-up's password is right.

steps.anchor: #define OPEN_MS (10 * 60 * 1000) /* a grown-up's password keeps it open this long */
steps.say: Once typed, the password keeps the computer open to the grown-up for ten minutes.

steps.anchor: static bool family_errand(int fd, const char *id, const char *cmd, const char *arg) {
steps.say: The desktop runs as the child, so it never decides alone. The lock and the password are kept and checked by init, as root, through the errands of lesson 05.
Each locked place asks the same question, `family_locks`, with one letter for what it guards. Here 's' guards Settings.
The lock screen works the same way: whether there is a password, and whether a guess is right, is asked of init.
